articles.title: Epilepsy: Summer Gigs, Seizures, and Stigma
articles.author: Dariya Yerkinbayeva · NIS PhM Almaty
articles.preview: The rumours reached me in the back of a taxi. My friend relegated, in gory details, the story of her classmates supporting a child through an epileptic seizure — and the stunted reaction that could have been disastrous.
articles.content:
In retrospect, the whispers were inevitable. They slithered around during break, clung to your clothes on the way home, and spilled out frightfully to classmates, eager to occupy more worried minds. The rumours reached me in the back of a taxi. My friend relegated, in gory details, the story of her classmates supporting a child through an epileptic seizure. Much like her, I was horrified. The cause of my shock, though, wasn’t the vivid description of blood and shaking — I was used to those — but the stunted reaction and lack of knowledgeability that could have been disastrous.

The seven-year-old was playing outside on a hot summer day at a summer camp when the seizure began. One of the teenage caretakers had the presence of mind to lower the child onto the ground and protect their head, knowledge that he credits to playing videogames. “The disclaimers at the start of the games, like ‘this might be dangerous for people with epilepsy,’ made me curious about seizures in general…” Tair Zhasbolat, NIS PhM ’26 said. The vast majority of caretakers, however, had no prior exposure to epilepsy whatsoever, despite it being the most common neurological condition in Kazakhstan. “We just didn’t know what to do,” an anonymous source recalled, and it was just pure luck that a random passerby swooped in: taking the child’s shoes and socks off, calling an ambulance. This unfortunate incident — a confrontation between lack of awareness and pure chance — is what pushed me to consider the cultural perception of epilepsy.

In the same year of 2024, a study was published at Nazarbayev University, reporting a significant increase in the incidence of epilepsy from 26.15 in 2014 to 88.80 in 2020 per 100,000 people in Kazakhstan. The same upwards trend was observed in prevalence rates and all-cause mortality. Beyond this quantitative data, not much else is known about epilepsy in Kazakhstan. Stigma, intertwined with both cultural and social factors, comprehensive legal framework, disability rights, as well as general visibility are still at a very low level. Moreover, there is a significant research gap centering epilepsy, as the abovementioned study is the first, most extensive, and comprehensive Central Asian epilepsy study.

Most people’s exposure to the condition is limited at best, with most interviewees citing trigger warnings on media, social media tags, and in rare cases, personal experiences as sources. This speaks volumes about the lack of awareness and veil of secrecy around epilepsy, considering that over 65 million people around the globe are diagnosed with epilepsy, and close to 80% live in economically backward and developing countries. Contrary to common diseases like asthma, diabetes, and heart disease, epilepsy remains one of the most misunderstood and neglected ones.

What Is Epilepsy?

Epilepsy is defined as a chronic brain disorder in which groups of nerve cells, or neurons, in the brain sometimes send the wrong signals and cause seizures. An important distinction is that while all epilepsy involves seizures, not all seizures point to epilepsy. Seizures occur when many neurons fire signals in quick succession at the same time, causing excessive electrical activity in the brain that may cause a range of involuntary movements, sensations, emotions, and/or behaviors.

A crucial aspect is the fact that it manifests in various ways across various populations and is dependent on a variety of factors. A primary factor is the location of neuron signalling in the brain; the brain’s cerebrum is divided into four lobes — frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital — each with specialised functions. So, if spontaneous electrical activity occurs in the parietal lobe, which is responsible for pressure response and spatial awareness, the seizure may include sensory symptoms such as tingling, numbness, and pain. Sometimes, however, seizures become generalised when faulty signalling spreads to other parts of the cerebrum, causing the range of symptoms we are most familiar with: foaming at the mouth, muscle stiffening and jerking.

Some people may experience loss of consciousness, some may stay aware while staring into space and making involuntary sounds, while others stay completely silent. This diversity makes the condition deeply complex, with a wide range of causes and types.

Stigma and Its Effects

Depending on the severity and frequency of epileptic seizures, people experience prejudice surrounding the condition. Stigma — as a powerful social construct, especially illness-related stigma — can have potent effects on a person’s life, hijacking their economic status, psychological wellbeing, social interactions and overall health. It pushes them to bear the additional cost of the illness, the inherent devaluation of personhood caused by the underlying disgrace, negative stereotyping, and social isolation. Stigma is classified into enacted and felt stigma, a distinction Scrambler and Hopkins make in their research.

The Legal Landscape in Kazakhstan

Kazakhstan has implemented laws that protect disability rights, primarily under the “On Social Protection of Persons with Disabilities,” and Labor Code Article 25 which prohibits restricting the right to conclude an employment contract based on disability, unless the state of health officially prevents the performance of duties. That being said, people with epilepsy are often neglected due to Kazakhstan’s strict “Disability Group” categorisation (1, 2, or 3), determined by a state medical-social commission. If people with epilepsy do not meet the standard for a certain degree of disability, they face the risk of losing legal protection in the workforce — increasing the occurrence of enacted stigma.

Cultural Factors

Beyond legislation, cultural factors play an important role in felt stigma. The most common response to epilepsy is thorough concealment. Increased secrecy prevents struggling people from receiving proper medical attention and care, which in turn causes people to turn to traditional medicine, religious figures, and social isolation, guided by shame and fear (uyat — a cultural code of values that symbolises a long tradition of acceptable moral-ethical conduct in Central Asian society). In some cases, epilepsy is interpreted as having supernatural causes, such as the “evil eye” or spiritual interference, which only reinforces the belief that the condition must be concealed at all costs.

What to Do If Someone Has a Seizure

In honour of March 26th — Purple Day, or International Epilepsy Awareness Day — it is of the utmost importance to continue speaking out about the invisible barriers of living with epilepsy in Kazakhstan. Witnessing someone have a seizure can be very scary and stressful, but being prepared and knowledgeable certainly softens the experience. Here is what to do:

  • Only move them if they’re in danger, such as near a busy road or hot cooker
  • Cushion their head if they’re on the ground
  • Loosen any tight clothing around their neck, such as a collar or tie, to aid breathing
  • Turn them on to their side after their convulsions stop (recovery position)
  • Stay with them and talk to them calmly until they recover
  • Note the time the seizure starts and finishes
  • If the person is in a wheelchair, put the brakes on and leave any seatbelt or harness on. Support them gently and cushion their head, but do not try to move them
  • Do not put anything in their mouth, including your fingers. They should not have any food or drink until they have fully recovered

Call emergency services if:

  • The person has been unconscious for more than 5 minutes
  • It’s the first time someone has had a seizure
  • The person is seriously injured during the seizure
  • The person has difficulty breathing after the seizure

It is also very helpful to record details about the seizure: what the person was doing beforehand, whether they mentioned any unusual sensations, any mood change, how attention was drawn to the seizure, whether there was loss of consciousness, any changes in colour, which body parts stiffened or twitched, and how the person was in recovery. This information is invaluable for medical professionals.

To me, epilepsy has never been about numbers on a screen or a comprehensive list of symptoms. To me, as someone whose whole life has been shrouded in secrecy and shame as a consequence of a family member grappling with epilepsy, epilepsy means real people’s lives in jeopardy because of cruelly false narratives.

Underneath the stigma and misunderstanding is a person that strains under the weight of “otherness” — an alienation that fills every corner of an otherwise happy life with uyat. I urge anyone reading this article to take the time to learn more about epilepsy with the intention to help just one single person feel just a little lighter, a little more prepared, and a little more accepted.

References
  1. Raising Awareness for All Types of Seizures — epilepsy.com (2024)
  2. Epilepsy in Women — epilepsy.com (2025)
  3. Epilepsy Awareness: Recognizing Seizures and Promoting Safety — Atlanta Neuro Institute (2023)
  4. Confronting the Stigma of Epilepsy — PMC (2011)
  5. How to Treat Epilepsy in Kazakhstan — MedSolution (2024)
  6. Epilepsy and Seizures — NINDS (2026)
  7. What to do if someone has a seizure — NHS UK (2024)
  8. What is Epilepsy? — The Ottawa Hospital (2023)

articles.title: Queer in 2026: Brilliant, Bold, Burroughs
articles.author: Dariya Yerkinbayeva · NIS PhM Almaty
articles.preview: It’s been weeks since I finished Queer by William S. Burroughs. Yet here I am, endlessly perusing Stanford Library’s Allen Ginsberg collection, wondering if the answer to the litany of issues threatening to crush us four decades later is Burroughs.
articles.content:
"... killing of species as beautiful as we, and explosions of science rockets, greenhouse earth warming predictions, the absolute or relative absolute bomb in our hands, Ukrainian wheat field radiation, AIDS, overpopulation, preachers claiming the exclusive word of god…we may be assured that Mr Burroughs will apply the great machine of his imagination to all these problems which I hope, and expect, and I’m sure will be touched on, one way or another this evening."

It’s been weeks since I finished Queer by William S. Burroughs. Yet here I am, endlessly perusing Stanford Library’s Allen Ginsberg collection, my eyes drooping shut when I stumble upon Ginsberg’s authoritative and solemn voice. This 1986 introduction momentarily captivates my attention, and I sit wondering if the answer to the litany of issues threatening to crush us four decades later, once again, is Burroughs.

After finishing Patti Smith’s celebrated memoir “Just Kids,” I picked up Burroughs in a flailing attempt to sink back into the gritty, experimental, and unequivocally creative scene of mid 20th-century New York City. I was intrigued by Smith’s apt (as I would later realize) description “William Burroughs was simultaneously old and young. Part sheriff, part gumshoe. All writer,” so I plunged into the world of Queer. I was counting on Burroughs to distract me with his dry humor, his simple truths, and signature revolting imagery. Instead, Lee Miller, the main character of the novella, launched into one of his routines and spat me right back out into 2026.

As Oliver Harris puts it in his introduction, this work marks a departure for Burroughs: an emotional departure from the accidental killing of his wife Joan Vollmer alongside a transformation of his writing technique into the cut-up method he is known for today. Queer is a spiraling departure from the real world into the “great machine” of William’s imagination, where politics and his personhood clash in a deadly embrace — a coiled snake, poisonous yet vulnerable. At its core, Queer is a revolt. It is a struggle, Burroughs shows, a revolution against the very essence of the Un-American.

The historical context of the novel is crucial to understanding its themes, as they’re weaved into the depths of this personal and collective reflection. The Cold War, rampant homophobia, the AIDS crisis, political propaganda, and radical conformity as a survival strategy… a landmark text, published in 1951 under a pseudonym Donald Webster Cory’s The Homosexual in America: A Subjective Approach was indicative of the era’s rigid expectations of the queer community. Cory argued for sympathy for the oppressor, forgiveness, quiet assimilation. His contemporary, Burroughs, was about to deliver anything but. You see, the book does not urge you to sympathize with Lee — it blatantly bashes him. It isn’t hard. Lee is obnoxious, even on the surface, prone to launch into his routines or unlikely stories that expose his disgustingly perverse desires of domination and control. The main manifestation of this is, of course, in the relationship between Lee and Allerton. Allerton’s character is young, strikingly beautiful, and perpetually bored, in other words, brimming with life. This quality makes him the perfect subject for Lee, as he seeks to control beauty personified, tainting it with his own depravity.

A person drowning in his own shame, Lee is simply unable to recognize the depth of his corruption, the resolute wrongness of it all. For there is no one in the world capable of “claiming the exclusive word of god.” And I believe this is the point that Burroughs was trying to make, one that so many miss. Lee’s character is an abomination, both a physical and spiritual danger to American society; he is a most formidable opponent, for he is blinded by righteousness. In fact, he is the American; an amalgamation of every poisonous quality, all the hate and fear that makes America, America trapped inside the body of a Queer Man — an antithesis in the cultural zeitgeist of the ’50s. Lee operates from a place of hunger, a void that urges to be recognized. In my interpretation, the cancerous desire to control is a direct reflection of the discrimination faced by the LGBTQ+ community, one that continues in the modern age, at least in my reality. Echoing Russia’s 2022 expansion of their anti-LGBTQ+ laws, on November 12th 2025, Kazakhstan’s parliament passed a bill to ban the promotion of so-called “non-traditional sexual orientation” in media and public spaces, which of course, includes literature. In the same way that queer people were scared into complacency by the lavender scare then, and continue to be stripped of their autonomy now, Burroughs calls out this disgraceful power-play through Lee. His character now takes on the role of oppressor, disrespecting the sacredness of choice, freedom, and love.

Perhaps due to Burroughs’ own personal politics of Violence v. Violence or his conviction to make his message crystal clear, he paints Lee not with empathy, but with detestation. In my interpretation, leaving Lee vulnerable and pathetic, painting him as a rejected, lonely, and shuddering being is an intentional choice. There is no absolution for him.

In his own way, Burroughs argues for a complex perspective on the world and the hate that fills it. He shows us the truth behind both sides, the ‘queers and the status quo’, demonstrating how futile the fight really is. It’s more than that, really, because not only is the fight utterly meaningless, it is void and disappointing, mirroring the final scene in the novel that offers no grand metaphor, no closure, no answer. To me, this is where the novel’s relevance lies. In times of uncertainty, I urge to remember Burroughs and his powerful work that reconciles painful honesty with honest pain. Underlined by Luca Guadagnino’s 2024 adaptation, starring Daniel Craig and Drew Starkey, Queer is not simply an empty ending, it’s our reality, deliciously popping with color, metaphors, and truth. It’s intimate. It’s raw. It’s beautifully queer in all senses of the word. Queer, the adjective, noun, verb, political identity.

articles.title: The Ground We Stand Upon: Urban Soil Pollution by Heavy Metals in Almaty
articles.author: Dariya Yerkinbayeva · NIS PhM Almaty
articles.preview: Almost two winters ago, I picked up my phone to check airkaz.org before heading out for the day. Poisonously purple numbers, well over in the triple digits, stared back at me. I wondered then if the air pollution was the only hidden threat to my hometown.
articles.content:
My hometown, Almaty, continues to be considered the cultural, industrial, historical and financial center of Kazakhstan, famous for its juicy apples, picturesque views, and legendary traffic. Not featured in postcards, this is the reality for most locals: hours lost to rush hour daily, a perpetual smog enveloping the city, a silent killer.

Almost two winters ago, I picked up my phone to check airkaz.org — a website that monitors air quality — before heading out for the day. Poisonously purple numbers, well over in the triple digits, stared back at me. I wondered then if the air pollution was the only hidden threat to my hometown.

A couple months later, I partnered up with Renata Batalova at NIS PhM, Professor Vassilios Inglezakis at the University of Strathclyde, and Professor Azat Seitkhan at Satbayev University to investigate the soil pollution in Almaty, more specifically urban soil pollution by heavy metals. We co-authored a research paper entitled: Urban Soil Pollution by Heavy Metals Cu, Ni, Zn, in Almaty, Kazakhstan in late summer of 2025. To access the full paper, you are more than welcome to reach either of us at dariyaadletovna@gmail.com or batalova.r.08@gmail.com and we will be happy to provide the document and discuss our findings.

Now, it is of the utmost importance to me to note the severity and distribution of this issue, as it affects a multitude of different facets of the local community’s livelihoods. Heavy metals, which are known to be extremely toxic and bioaccumulative are a big concern for environmental safety. Especially in their soluble phase, they have a detrimental effect on human health, plant activity and soil productivity. In a 2020 study on non-carcinogen and carcinogenic risk assessment of five heavy metals (Pb, Cd, Cu, Zn, and Cr) in the soils of Almaty, results confirmed that both adults and children exceeded the threshold of carcinogenic assessment (with cancer risks ranging from 1×10⁻⁶ and 5×10⁻⁶, respectively) proving the urgent need for soil remediation.

Another danger lies in the substantial uptake of heavy metals by plants through atmospheric deposition, root system and foliage in relation to traffic and industrial activity. This is a serious environmental problem, since elevated contents of heavy metals in plants leads to accumulation in the tissues of organisms, eventually reaching humans through food chains. These metals might also be easily transferred to humans by inhalation, ingestion and/or dermal absorption which leads to accumulation in fatty tissues due to non-degradability, further causing potential health risks affecting the nervous, endocrine, immune systems, hematopoietic function, normal cellular metabolism, etc. It is also very important to consider the fact that parks, gardens, playgrounds, schools, and kindergartens located in the busy city are a direct public health risk to children because of common behaviours such as hand or finger sucking that are considered the key pathways for ingestion of toxins.

Research Methodology

As part of our research, we collected soil samples from 4 representative sites located 10 to 20 m from the targeted roads, which were determined by traffic volume and proximity to thermal plants. The first site was a key intersection between Dostyk and Abay Avenue, where significant traffic congestion was recorded. The next sample was taken at Zelyony Bazaar, a central shopping destination that attracts traffic daily and is in close proximity to Rakhat, a confectionary factory. The third site was the intersection of Zhambyl Street and Al-Farabi Avenue, since it is in close proximity to one of three thermal plants located within city bounds. The final site was Severnoe Koltzo, a highway that serves as a road to the city for many workers who live in smaller neighbouring towns.

Surface sampling was performed and soil samples were analyzed at the Laboratory of Engineering profile at Satbayev University using the VANTA Element-s analyzer. Standard chemical analysis reported the following:

  • The Zn concentration was 1300 ppm which is 56 times the normative amount at 23 ppm
  • The Cu concentration peaked at 560 ppm which exceeds the normative by 17 times at 33 ppm
  • The Ni concentration was the most evenly distributed with a range of 710–850 ppm which exceeds the normative by 212 times at 4 ppm

According to previous research recognized in this field, all heavy metals that were being investigated are likely to have originated from anthropogenic sources, such as industrial processes, vehicular traffic intensity, and many more. In this case, we theorized that the unregulated and intense traffic, and possible improper disposal of wastes nearby the thermal plant and chocolate factory could be the reason for such high concentrations.

Almaty’s Traffic Problem

As mentioned above, Almaty is infamous for its increasingly serious traffic congestion problem, with the amount of registered personal vehicles exceeding 700 thousand with an additional flow of over 230 thousand vehicles from the suburbs amounting to over 1 million cars in the city per day. Most vehicles in Almaty operate on gasoline that contains tetraethyl lead as an additive and general low-quality gasoline which are proven to be correlated to high concentrations of lead in soils. Not to mention the geographical placement of Almaty at the foothills of the Trans-Ili Alatau mountains, a factor that exacerbates the city’s environmental problems, as it limits the wind flow and traps toxic gasses from industrial activities.

Health Risks

Long term exposure to toxic heavy metals, even in comparatively small concentrations, can lead to public health risks: ingestion and accumulation of Pb in the body can adversely affect the nervous system, as well as lead to kidney failure. Exposure to Cu might lead to lung cancer, while excessive intake increases health risks associated with the central nervous system, kidney and liver function. Pb is also toxic, since it may damage the nervous system manifesting through memory loss, headaches, insomnia, and cause renal failure in the case of critically high consumption. Although the repercussions of soil contamination by heavy metals are severe not only for public health, but for infrastructure development — since soils provide stable structural bases — road stability, waste disposal efficiency, the agriculture sector’s productivity, and healthy microbial life.

A Call for Action

It is very upsetting and truly alarming that no codex has been applied to protect soils from heavy metal contamination, despite the issue’s urgent character. Industrialization and economic prosperity are often prioritized over environmental protection, so this is largely unsurprising, albeit disappointing. It is precisely due to the lack of legislation and funding regarding metal concentrations in roadside dust and urban soils that studies conducted in this field are so few and, for the most part, outdated. Detailed research on pollution by heavy metals in the context of the local industrial scene is necessary, not only for Almaty, but for other major cities in Kazakhstan.

Effective measures must be taken to control the pollution of soils, and by association water sources and biochemical processes integral to sustainable development, by the abovementioned heavy metals. Introducing countermeasures, such as controlling the number of vehicles on highways, and making adjustments in the industry sphere, like reevaluating urban/suburban factories’ locations, reducing power consumption, developing effective pollution discharge reduction strategies, and overall optimization of major industrial structures of the city is absolutely necessary.

References
  1. Admimalla, S., & Wang, J. (2018). Human health risk assessment of heavy metals in soil. Environmental Science and Pollution Research, 25(26).
  2. Ajmone-Marsan, F., & Biasioli, M. (2010). Trace elements in soils. Environmental Science and Pollution Research, 17(2).
  3. Alloway, B. J. (2013). Heavy metals in soils: trace metals and metalloids in soils and their bioavailability. Springer.
  4. Ramazanova, R., et al. (2020). Assessment of non-carcinogenic and carcinogenic risks of heavy metals in soils of Almaty. Eurasian Soil Science, 53(11).
  5. Madibekov, A., et al. (2023). Air pollution from vehicles in Almaty city. Transportation Research Procedia, 68.
  6. Kabata-Pendias, A., & Pendias, H. (2001). Trace elements in soils and plants. CRC Press.
  7. Chen, T. B., et al. (2005). Accumulation of heavy metals in urban soils in Hong Kong. Environmental International, 31(7).
  8. Rakhimbaev, K., et al. (2023). Analysis of traffic congestion in Almaty and proposed solutions. Journal of Eastern European and Central Asian Research, 10(1).
